payload.name: thyroid-cartilage
payload.scope: People made the thyroid cartilage construct to identify the paired laryngeal cartilage forming the anterior framework of the larynx and housing the vocal folds, so that clinicians can locate it for surgical landmarks, airway access, and voice disorder treatment.

definition.body: The thyroid cartilage is the human-authored anatomical construct identifying the paired laminae that fuse anteriorly to form the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple) and provide the anterior and lateral framework of the larynx, anchoring the vocal folds and intrinsic muscles. Parameters: (1) the laminae — two quadrilateral plates that meet at the anterior median angle; (2) the laryngeal prominence — the anterior ridge formed by the superior and inferior thyroid crests, palpable as the Adam's apple; (3) the superior and inferior horns — posterior extensions of each lamina providing attachment points for ligaments and membranes; (4) the external surface — attachments for the sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, and inferior constrictor muscles; (5) the internal surface — attachments for the thyrohyoid membrane and the vocal ligament. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, laryngology, and airway management, providing the structural referent for laryngeal framework surgery, tracheostomy, and laryngoplasty procedures. e.g.: the thyroid cartilage anatomy shown in Gray's Anatomy, 51st edition; the laryngeal prominence palpated during thyroid examination per Bates' Guide to Physical Examination; open laryngectomy with thyroid cartilage resection for advanced glottic cancer per the VA Laryngeal Cancer Study | not: the cricoid cartilage (complete ring-shaped cartilage below the thyroid); the thyroid gland (endocrine organ, distinct from laryngeal cartilage) [formal: cartilago thyroidea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cricoid-cartilage
payload.scope: People made the cricoid cartilage construct to identify the complete ring-shaped cartilage forming the inferior-most structural component of the laryngeal framework, so that clinicians can locate this critical landmark for emergency surgical airway access and airway management procedures.

definition.body: The cricoid cartilage is the human-authored anatomical construct identifying the complete ring-shaped cartilage forming the inferior-most component of the laryngeal framework, whose posterior lamina is taller than the anterior arch and whose articular facets receive the arytenoid cartilages superiorly. Parameters: (1) the anterior arch — a narrow curved band approximately 2.5 cm high, providing attachment for several strap muscles and the cricothyroid ligament; (2) the posterior lamina — a broad plate approximately 3-4 cm high, presenting superior articular facets for the arytenoid cartilages on each side; (3) the lateral surfaces — each presenting superior and inferior cricothyroid articular facets for the inferior horns of the thyroid cartilage; (4) the superior border — continuous with the inferior margin of the thyroid cartilage via the cricothyroid membrane, and bearing the superior cricoarytenoid muscle attachment; (5) the inferior border — continuous with the first tracheal ring via the cricotracheal ligament. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, airway management protocols, and head-and-neck surgical planning. e.g.: the cricoid cartilage as illustrated in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; the cricothyroidotomy landmark per ATLS guidelines for emergency surgical airway access; cricoid pressure (Sellick technique) applied during rapid sequence intubation per Bailey & Love | not: the cricoid membrane (the fibrous band connecting the cricoid to the thyroid cartilage, not the cartilage itself); the cricothyroid membrane (the elastic connective tissue between thyroid and cricoid, not a cartilaginous structure) [formal: cartilago cricoidea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The epiglottic cartilage is the human-authored anatomical construct identifying the leaf-shaped elastic cartilage situated at the superior aspect of the laryngeal inlet, whose flexible leaf folds posteriorly during swallowing to protect the airway from aspiration. Parameters: (1) the lamina — a thin flattened plate approximately 4-5 cm long, with a superior epiglottic surface exposed to the vallecula and a posterior laryngeal surface facing the laryngeal inlet; (2) the stalk (petiolus) — a narrower inferior attachment connecting the lamina to the posterior surface of the thyroid cartilage at the angle, forming the epiglottic cartilage angle; (3) the associated structures — the median epiglottic fold connecting to the thyroid cartilage, the two lateral epiglottic folds merging with the aryepiglottic folds, and the paired epiglottic (vallecular) glands; (4) the cartilaginous core — elastic cartilage with type II collagen fibers providing flexibility while maintaining structural integrity through repeated flexion cycles; (5) the sensory innervation — the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve provides afferent fibers to the laryngeal surface, triggering the epiglottic reflex and contributing to the cough reflex. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, airway management protocols, and otolaryngological surgical planning. e.g.: the epiglottis as depicted in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; the direct laryngoscopy view showing epiglottic leaflet retraction per ATLS guidelines; the modified Wilson technique using epiglottic elevation per Bailey & Love | not: the epiglottis (the anatomical structure itself, not the anatomical construct); the vallecula (the depression between the tongue base and epiglottis, a space not a cartilage) [formal: cartilago epiglottica | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cricoid-cartilage
payload.scope: People made the cricoid cartilage construct to map and categorize the complete ring-shaped cartilage below the arytenoid cartilages at the inferior aspect of the larynx, so that surgeons can identify this critical landmark for airway management, tracheostomy, and laryngeal surgery.

definition.body: The cricoid cartilage is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the complete ring-shaped cartilage forming the inferior framework of the larynx, whose posterior lamina and anterior arch define the boundary between larynx and trachea. Parameters: (1) the anterior arch — a narrow curved band approximately 6 mm high, continuous posteriorly with the lamina; (2) the posterior lamina — a broad flat plate extending superiorly to articulate with the arytenoid cartilages; (3) the articular facets — the cricothyroid facet on the inferior lateral surface for articulation with the thyroid cartilage, and the cricoarytenoid facet on the superior lateral surface for articulation with the arytenoid cartilage base. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, laryngology classification systems, and surgical planning documents. e.g.: the cricoid cartilage anatomy described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; the cricoid tear-drop shape on lateral neck radiograph as a landmark for cricothyrotomy; the cricoid cartilage dimensions measured in the cadaveric study by Skoog (1963) | not: the cricoid membrane (the elastic tissue connecting cricoid to thyroid cartilage, not the cartilage itself); the tracheal rings (C-shaped cartilages below the cricoid, separated by the cricotracheal ligament) [formal: cartilago cricoidea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: thyroid-cartilage
payload.scope: People made the thyroid cartilage construct to map and categorize the largest cartilage of the larynx, so that surgeons can identify this landmark for airway management, laryngeal surgery, and procedures such as cricothyrotomy.

definition.body: The thyroid cartilage is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired laminae forming the largest cartilage of the larynx, whose anterior fusion creates the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple) and whose framework houses and protects the vocal folds. Parameters: (1) the paired laminae — two rectangular plates that fuse anteriorly at varying angles (sharper in males ~90°, more obtuse in females ~120°); (2) the laryngeal prominence — the anterior projection at the junction of the two laminae, more prominent in adult males; (3) the superior and inferior horns — posterior extensions from each lamina, the superior horn attached to the hyoid bone by the middle thyrohyoid ligament and the inferior horn articulating with the cricoid cartilage; (4) the articular facets — the cricothyroid facet on the inferior horn's lateral surface and the oblique line on the lamina's anterolateral surface for muscle attachments. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, laryngology classification systems, and surgical planning documents. e.g.: the thyroid cartilage anatomy described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; the laryngeal prominence palpated during neck examination as a surface landmark; the thyroid cartilage fracture assessed on CT imaging after blunt neck trauma | not: the thyroid gland (the endocrine organ anterior and inferior to the thyroid cartilage, unrelated cartilage); the thyrohyoid membrane (the fibrous sheet between thyroid cartilage and hyoid bone, not the cartilage itself) [formal: cartilago thyroidea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The epiglottic cartilage is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the leaf-shaped elastic cartilage situated at the superior entrance of the larynx, whose role in covering the glottis during swallowing protects the airway from aspiration. Parameters: (1) the lamina — a thin flat plate of elastic cartilage approximately 4 cm long, with a free upper border and a narrowed stem attached to the thyroid cartilage angle; (2) the surface anatomy — the lingual surface (anterior, facing the root of the tongue) and the laryngeal surface (posterior, facing the laryngeal inlet); (3) the attachment — the epiglottic stalk attached to the posterior surface of the thyroid cartilage at an angle of approximately 40 degrees in adults. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, emergency airway management protocols, and laryngology atlases. e.g.: the epiglottic cartilage described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; the epiglottis visible on direct laryngoscopy as a landmark for endotracheal intubation; the epiglottic shape on lateral neck radiograph in a child | not: the epiglottis (the entire anatomical structure including mucosa, not just the cartilage construct); the aryepiglottic fold (mucosal fold with elastic cartilage, a distinct structure) [formal: cartilago epiglottica | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: recurrent-laryngeal-nerve
payload.scope: People made the recurrent laryngeal nerve construct to map and categorize the branch of the vagus nerve that supplies motor and sensory innervation to all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid, so that surgeons can avoid injury during thyroidectomy and clinicians can diagnose laryngeal neuropathies.

definition.body: The recurrent laryngeal nerve is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the branch of the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) that ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove to innervate all intrinsic laryngeal muscles and provide sensory input to the laryngeal mucosa below the vocal folds. Parameters: (1) the recurrent course — the right nerve hooks under the right subclavian artery and ascends vertically; the left nerve loops under the aortic arch lateral to the ligamentum arteriosum before ascending — a difference arising from embryological migration of the arch arteries; (2) the sensory distribution — supplies mucosa of the larynx inferior to the vocal folds, including the piriform fossa; (3) the motor distribution — innervates the posterior cricoarytenoid (abductor), lateral cricoarytenoid (adductor), thyroarytenoid (relaxer), vocalis (fine-tuner), and interarytenoid (adductor) muscles; (4) the anatomical course — ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove between the trachea and esophagus, entering the larynx posterior to the inferior constrictor. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in surgical anatomy texts, thyroidectomy protocols, and laryngology atlases. e.g.: the recurrent laryngeal nerve course described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; the recurrent laryngeal nerve identified and preserved during total thyroidectomy per the Carnavit vessel-tie technique; the right and left recurrent laryngeal nerve asymmetry documented in the embryological study by Tandler (1898) | not: the superior-laryngeal-nerve (branches directly from the vagus at the inferior ganglion and has a non-recurrent course); the vagus-nerve (the parent cranial nerve from which the recurrent laryngeal nerve branches) [formal: nervus laryngeus recurrens | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: aryepiglottic-fold
payload.scope: People made the aryepiglottic fold construct to map and categorize the mucosal fold containing elastic cartilage that extends from the arytenoid cartilages to the epiglottis, so that clinicians can identify the lateral boundaries of the laryngeal inlet during airway management.

definition.body: The aryepiglottic fold is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired mucosal folds extending from the lateral margins of the epiglottis to the apex of each arytenoid cartilage, forming the superior and lateral boundaries of the laryngeal inlet and containing elastic cartilage within its substance. Parameters: (1) the mucosal surface — smooth mucosa continuous with the laryngeal vestibule, forming a visible ridge on endoscopy; (2) the contained cartilage — the corniculate cartilage at the apex of each fold and the cuneiform cartilage embedded within the fold's substance (not present in all individuals); (3) the sensory function — the fold's mucosa contains sensory endings that trigger the cough reflex when stimulated; (4) the sphincteric mechanism — the fold contributes to the sphincteric closure of the laryngeal inlet during swallowing and airway protection. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in laryngology atlases, emergency airway management protocols, and endoscopy references. e.g.: the aryepiglottic fold as the lateral boundary of the laryngeal inlet on fiberoptic laryngoscopy; the aryepiglottic fold containing the cuneiform cartilage described in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; the aryepiglottic pleats palpated during digital examination for epiglottitis | not: the aryepiglottic ligament (the elastic cartilage core without the overlying mucosa, not the complete fold); the pyriform fossa (the mucosal depression lateral to the aryepiglottic fold, a separate space) [formal: plicae aryepiglotticae | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The interarytenoid muscle is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the unpaired intrinsic laryngeal muscle spanning between the two arytenoid cartilages posterior to the glottis, whose contraction adducts the arytenoids and narrows the posterior glottic chink. Parameters: (1) the oblique fibers — the most important portion, extending from the muscular process of one arytenoid to the apex and lateral margin of the opposite arytenoid, crossing in a diagonal fashion; (2) the transverse fibers — a shallow layer spanning the posterior surfaces of both arytenoids without crossing; (3) the action — pulls the arytenoid cartilages toward each other, approximating their vocal processes and narrowing the posterior glottic aperture; (4) the functional role — primary adductor of the posterior glottis, working with the lateral cricoarytenoid muscles for complete vocal fold closure, and contributing to airway protection during swallowing. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, laryngology classification systems, and surgical anatomy references. e.g.: the interarytenoid muscle described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; the interarytenoid muscle identified during posterior laryngoscopy as a bulge between the arytenoids; the interarytenoid atrophy noted in unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy | not: the lateral-cricoarytenoid-muscle (adducts the vocal folds but from the cricoid to the arytenoid, a distinct muscle); the posterior-cricoarytenoid-muscle (the abductor acting on the arytenoids from the opposite direction) [formal: muscular interarytaenoideum | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.scope: People made the lateral cricoarytenoid muscle construct to map and categorize the intrinsic laryngeal muscle that adducts the vocal folds by rotating the arytenoid cartilages inward, so that clinicians can understand vocal fold closure mechanics and diagnose glottic insufficiency.

definition.body: The lateral cricoarytenoid muscle is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired intrinsic laryngeal muscle originating from the cricoid cartilage and inserting on the arytenoid cartilage, whose contraction adducts the vocal folds by rotating the muscular processes medially. Parameters: (1) the origin — the upper margin and lateral surface of the cricoid cartilage arch; (2) the insertion — the muscular process and anterior border of the arytenoid cartilage; (3) the action — pulls the muscular process forward and medially, rotating the vocal process inward to adduct the vocal folds and close the posterior glottic aperture; (4) the innervation — by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, like all other intrinsic laryngeal muscles; (5) the functional relationship — works together with the interarytenoid muscle for complete posterior glottic closure. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, laryngology classification systems, and surgical anatomy references. e.g.: the lateral cricoarytenoid muscle described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake, Hauser and Carucci; the lateral cricoarytenoid injection laryngoplasty for unilateral vocal fold paralysis per Murray and Woodson; electromyographic assessment of lateral cricoarytenoid function per Johns Hopkins Voice Center protocols | not: the posterior cricoarytenoid muscle (opposes this muscle, abducting rather than adducting the vocal folds); the thyroarytenoid muscle (runs within the vocal fold wall, primarily relaxing rather than adducting) [formal: musculus cricoarytaenoideus lateralis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: vocalis-muscle
payload.scope: People made the vocalis muscle construct to map and categorize the deep medial fibers of the thyroarytenoid muscle that fine-tune vocal fold tension and stiffness independent of arytenoid rotation, so that clinicians can understand voice pitch control and diagnose intrinsic laryngeal muscle dysfunction.

definition.body: The vocalis muscle is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the deep medial portion of the thyroarytenoid muscle, composed of parallel fibers running alongside the vocal fold ligament, whose graded contraction fine-tunes vocal fold stiffness and tension independently of gross arytenoid rotation. Parameters: (1) the origin — the inner surface and angle of the thyroid cartilage; (2) the insertion — the vocal process and anterior margin of the arytenoid cartilage; (3) the layered relationship — lies deep within the vocal fold, immediately superficial to the vocal fold ligament and medial lamina propria; (4) the functional independence — can alter vocal fold stiffness locally without changing overall length, enabling independent control of tension and pitch; (5) the clinical relevance — vocalis atrophy or paresis contributes to glottic insufficiency and voice breathiness. It persists as a standard anatomical region in human anatomy texts, laryngology classification systems, and voice research protocols. e.g.: the vocalis muscle described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake, Hauser and Carucci; the vocal fold mucosal wave analyzed by high-speed videoendoscopy in Hirano's structural model; vocal fold medialization thyroplasty type I per Isshiki's classification | not: the thyroarytenoid muscle (the broader muscle of which the vocalis is the deep medial portion); the cricothyroid muscle (tenses the vocal fold from outside the fold wall) [formal: musculus vocalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cricothyroid-joint
payload.scope: People made the cricothyroid joint construct to map and categorize the synovial articulation between the cricoid and thyroid cartilages that enables the tilting motion which tenses the vocal folds, so that clinicians can understand laryngeal biomechanics relevant to voice production and cricothyrotomy procedures.

definition.body: The cricothyroid joint is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired synovial joints where the inferior horns of the thyroid cartilage articulate with corresponding facets on the cricoid cartilage, whose rotation and sliding movements enable the thyroid cartilage to tilt forward, thereby increasing tension on the vocal folds. Parameters: (1) the articulation — the cricothyroid articular facet on the lateral surface of the inferior horn of the thyroid cartilage against the corresponding facet on the cricoid cartilage; (2) the joint capsule — a thin fibrous capsule enclosing the articular surfaces; (3) the ligamentous support — the lateral cricothyroid ligament reinforcing the joint posteriorly; (4) the movement — rotation of the thyroid cartilage on the cricoid, increasing the distance between the thyroid notch and vocal processes; (5) the functional outcome — tilting the thyroid cartilage forward stretches the vocal ligament, raising vocal fold tension and pitch. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, laryngology classification systems, and surgical anatomy references. e.g.: the cricothyroid joint described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake, Hauser and Carucci; the cricothyroid joint movement demonstrated during pitch variation by Titze's voice laboratory protocols; the cricothyroid joint dislocation following blunt laryngeal trauma per Holinger's classification | not: the cricothyroid ligament (midline elastic tissue from cricoid to thyroid cartilage); the cricoarytenoid joint (articulation between cricoid and arytenoid cartilages) [formal: articulatio cricothyroides | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: vocal-ligament
payload.scope: People made the vocal ligament construct to identify the elastic fibrous band that forms the structural core of the vocal fold, so that clinicians and surgeons can localize the tissue plane for phonosurgical approaches and injection laryngoplasty.

definition.body: The vocal ligament is the human-authored anatomical construct identifying the paired elastic fibrous band that extends from the vocal process of the arytenoid cartilage anteriorly to the angle of the thyroid cartilage, forming the structural core of the vocal fold. Parameters: (1) the course — runs from the anterior vocal process to the thyroid angle at the midline; (2) the composition — dense connective tissue rich in elastic fibers; (3) the mechanical role — provides tensile strength to the vocal fold; (4) the surgical landmark — the plane where microlaryngeal instruments approach for excision or grafting. It persists as a standard surgical landmark in laryngology and phonosurgery. e.g.: Zeitels microflap technique for vocal fold lesions (Laryngoscope, 2008); Hirano's mucosal wave model of vocal fold vibration; PTV staging system for early glottic carcinoma | not: the cricothyroid ligament; the vocal fold [formal: ligamentum vocale | substrate: matter | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cricothyroid-membrane
payload.scope: People made the cricothyroid membrane construct to identify the thick elastic tissue between the cricoid and thyroid cartilages, so that clinicians can perform emergency surgical airway access and surgeons can plan laryngeal approaches.

definition.body: The cricothyroid membrane is the human-authored anatomical construct identifying the broad elastic fibrous sheet connecting the superior margin of the cricoid cartilage to the inferior margin of the thyroid cartilage anteriorly and laterally. Parameters: (1) the location — spans the gap between the cricoid arch anteriorly and the thyroid cartilage inferior horn, bounded medially by the cricothyroid ligament (median thyrohyoid membrane); (2) the composition — dense irregular connective tissue with elastic fibers, thicker and more compliant than the median cricothyroid ligament; (3) the vascular supply — the anterior and posterior superior laryngeal arteries from the superior thyroid artery; (4) the clinical landmark — the most superficial structure between the airway and the skin surface, targeted in emergency cricothyroidotomy; (5) the surgical access plane — the midline puncture or incision site for emergency surgical airway when endotracheal intubation is impossible. It persists as a standard emergency airway landmark in ATLS and anesthesia guidelines. e.g.: emergency cricothyroidotomy technique described in ATLS 10th edition protocols; cricothyroid membrane visualization during ultrasound-guided airway assessment; Seldinger technique cricothyroidotomy per the American Society of Anesthesiologists difficult airway algorithm | not: the cricothyroid ligament (the median elastic band at the midline, distinct from the broader membrane); the cricothyroid joint (the synovial articulation between cartilage facets posterior to the membrane) [formal: membrana cricothyroidea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The piriform fossa is the human-authored anatomical construct identifying the paired mucosal depressions flanking the laryngeal inlet, extending from the aryepiglottic folds superiorly to the postcricoid region inferiorly and bounded laterally by the thyroid cartilage. Parameters: (1) the boundaries — medial wall formed by the aryepiglottic fold and lateral cricoarytenoid muscle; lateral wall by the thyroid cartilage inner surface; (2) the mucosal lining — stratified squamous epithelium continuous with pharyngeal and esophageal mucosa; (3) the contents — the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the mucosa; (4) the clinical significance — common site for foreign body impaction and target for blind nasal intubation; (5) the surgical relevance — traversed during endoscopic approaches and important for metastatic spread from hypopharyngeal carcinoma. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in otolaryngology and gastroenterology. e.g.: piriform fossa foreign body impaction in Cummings Otolaryngology 6th edition; piriform fossa evaluation during swallowing videofluoroscopy; piriform fossa innervation by the internal laryngeal nerve in anesthesia texts [not: the piriform sinus; the epiglottis [formal: sinus piriformis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: laryngopharynx
payload.scope: People made the laryngopharynx construct to identify the lowest region of the pharynx continuous with the esophagus, so that clinicians can plan swallowing assessments and surgical access to the hypopharynx.

definition.body: The laryngopharynx is the human-authored anatomical construct identifying the inferior portion of the pharynx extending from the epiglottis superiorly to the esophagus inferiorly, and from the aryepiglottic folds laterally. Parameters: (1) the boundaries — extends from the upper border of the epiglottis to the lower border of the cricoid cartilage at C6 level; (2) the subdivisions — the piriform fossae laterally and the postcricoid region anteriorly; (3) the mucosal lining — stratified squamous epithelium continuous with the esophagus; (4) the functional role — shared conduit for respiratory and digestive tracts with the laryngeal inlet opening anteriorly; (5) the clinical significance — site of hypopharyngeal carcinoma and key region in swallow mechanics. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in otolaryngology and gastroenterology. e.g.: laryngopharynx anatomy in Cummings Otolaryngology 6th edition; postcricoid region in videofluoroscopic swallow study; hypopharyngeal carcinoma in AJCC 8th edition [not: the oropharynx; the esophagus [formal: pharynx laryngea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cuneiform-cartilage
payload.scope: People made the cuneiform cartilage construct to identify the paired elastic nodules within the aryepiglottic folds, so that clinicians can palpate abnormalities and radiologists can localise cysts during laryngeal imaging.

definition.body: The cuneiform cartilage is the human-authored anatomical construct identifying the paired unpaired cartilaginous nodules situated within the aryepiglottic folds, anterior to the arytenoid cartilages. Parameters: (1) the position — embedded within the aryepiglottic fold mucosa, medial to the corniculate cartilage and lateral to the epiglottis; (2) the composition — elastic cartilage continuous with the aryepiglottic fold; (3) the boundaries — extends from near the epiglottic apex posteriorly to the level of the arytenoid cartilage; (4) the clinical significance — site of cysts and tumors, palpable during indirect laryngoscopy as the aryepiglottic fold bulge; (5) the developmental note — may fuse with adjacent cartilages with age. payload.name: vocal-folds
payload.scope: People made the vocal folds construct to map the paired mucosal folds within the larynx that vibrate to produce voiced sound, serving as the primary sound source for human speech.

definition.body: Vocal folds are a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired mucosal folds within the laryngeal cavity, consisting of the vocalis muscle covered by epithelium and lined by lamina propria (vocal ligament, superficial and deep layers). Parameters: (1) the layered microstructure — epithelium, lamina propria with its superficial, intermediate, and deep layers (the vocal ligament), and the vocalis muscle; (2) the boundaries — extend from the angle of the thyroid cartilage anteriorly to the arytenoid cartilages posteriorly; (3) the functional division — the vibratory portion (cover: epithelium and superficial lamina propria) and the rigid portion (body: vocalis muscle and deep lamina propria); (4) the blood supply — laryngeal branches of the superior and inferior thyroid arteries; (5) the neural supply — recurrent laryngeal nerve branches to the vocalis muscle and sensory innervation above the folds. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in laryngology, phonetics, and airway management. e.g.: the vocal folds as described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; direct laryngoscopy visualization of the vocal fold mucosa; the mucosal wave theory of vocal fold vibration per Hirano's phoniatric classification | not: the vestibular folds (false vocal folds above the true vocal folds); the vocal tract (the resonant cavity above the larynx that shapes sound into speech) [formal: strumae vocales | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: carina
payload.scope: People made the carina construct to map the anatomical ridge at the tracheal bifurcation where the left and right main bronchi diverge, serving as a critical landmark for airway management and bronchoscopic localization.

definition.body: The carina is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the midline cartilaginous ridge at the inferior terminus of the tracheal lumen where it bifurcates into the left and right main bronchi. Parameters: (1) the anatomical position — located at the level of the T4–T5 intervertebral disc (sternal angle plane) in adults, slightly to the right of the midline; (2) the structural composition — hyaline cartilage plates within the tracheal wall at the bifurcation point, forming a sharp mucosal ridge; (3) the sensory function — densely innervated by vagal afferent fibers making it one of the most sensitive areas of the airway, triggering the cough reflex when stimulated; (4) the asymmetry — the left main bronchus diverges at a sharper angle (~70°) than the right (~25°), making aspiration more common on the right side; (5) the clinical significance — key landmark in bronchoscopy (marks the division between central and peripheral airways), endotracheal tube depth reference, and site of carinal disease (tumors, trauma). It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in radiology, pulmonology, and thoracic surgery. e.g.: the carina as described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; endobronchial ultrasound landmark at the tracheobronchial junction; carinal resection technique for bronchogenic carcinoma per Pearson's thoracic surgery | not: the trachea (the tubular airway above the carina, distinct structure); the larynx (the organ superior to the trachea housing the vocal folds, separate structure) [formal: carina tracheae | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: bronchus
payload.scope: People made the bronchus construct to map the major airway passages extending from the tracheal bifurcation into the lungs, serving as the primary conduit for air passage to the pulmonary parenchyma.

definition.body: The bronchus is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the major airway passages extending from the carina into the lungs, maintaining open lumens for air passage to the pulmonary parenchyma. Parameters: (1) the division — the right main bronchus (shorter, wider, more vertical) and the left main bronchus (longer, narrower, more horizontal), diverging from the carina at T4–T5 level; (2) the cartilaginous support — C-shaped or irregular hyaline cartilage plates in the walls, decreasing in number toward the periphery until absent at ~8th generation; (3) the mucosal lining — pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells, continuous with the tracheal lining; (4) the muscular component — bronchial smooth muscle (bronchialis) between cartilage plates, allowing bronchoconstriction and bronchodilation; (5) the segmental division — right lung has 10 bronchopulmonary segments (3 lobar, 7–10 segmental); left lung has 8–10 segments (2 lobar, 6–8 segmental). It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in pulmonology, radiology, and thoracic surgery. e.g.: the bronchus as described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; bronchoscopy visualization of the right main bronchus and its superior lobe ostium; bronchial artery embolization for hemoptysis per the Journal of Vascular and Interventional Radiology | not: the trachea (the airway above the bronchial bifurcation, distinct structure); the alveolus (the gas-exchange unit distal to the bronchial tree, smaller structure) [formal: bronchus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: epiglottis
payload.scope: People made the epiglottis construct to identify the leaf-shaped guard at the laryngeal inlet, so that airway clinicians can recognise the aspiration barrier during laryngoscopy, intubation, and epiglottitis assessment.

definition.body: The epiglottis is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the leaf-shaped structure at the laryngeal inlet that covers the glottis during swallowing and protects the airway from aspiration. Parameters: (1) the shape — a petal of elastic cartilage covered by mucosa, with a broad lingual surface facing the root of the tongue and a narrow laryngeal surface facing the laryngeal inlet; (2) the attachments — a stalk fixed to the thyroid cartilage by the thyroepiglottic ligament and a superior connection to the hyoid bone by the hyoepiglottic ligament; (3) the mucosal cover — stratified squamous epithelium continuous with the oropharyngeal mucosa on the lingual surface and the laryngeal mucosa on the laryngeal surface; (4) the function — epiglottic deflection during swallowing tilts the epiglottis over the laryngeal inlet and diverts the bolus around the piriform fossae; (5) the clinical significance — acute infection (epiglottitis) with airway obstruction, and the epiglottic position assessed on direct laryngoscopy and lateral neck radiograph. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in otolaryngology, airway management, and radiology. e.g.: the epiglottis as described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; the swollen epiglottis producing the thumb sign on lateral neck radiograph in acute epiglottitis; epiglottic deflection observed on flexible nasendoscopy during a videofluoroscopic swallow study | not: the epiglottic cartilage (the cartilage alone, without its mucosal cover); the aryepiglottic fold (the mucosal fold from the epiglottic apex to the arytenoid); the vestibular folds (the mucosal folds below the epiglottis in the laryngeal vestibule) [formal: epiglottis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: piriform-fossa
payload.scope: People made the piriform fossa construct to map the paired depressions flanking the laryngeal inlet, so that clinicians can localize foreign body impaction, recognize hypopharyngeal carcinoma, and plan surgical access to the hypopharynx.

definition.body: The piriform fossa is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the paired mucosal depressions flanking the laryngeal inlet, each extending from the aryepiglottic fold superiorly to the postcricoid region inferiorly and bounded laterally by the thyroid cartilage. Parameters: (1) the boundaries — the medial wall formed by the aryepiglottic fold and the lateral cricoarytenoid muscle, the lateral wall by the inner surface of the thyroid cartilage; (2) the mucosal lining — stratified squamous epithelium continuous with the pharyngeal and esophageal mucosa; (3) the innervation — the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies sensory innervation to the fossa's mucosa; (4) the clinical significance — a common site for foreign body impaction (fish bones), a region of the hypopharynx in TNM staging, and a landmark for blind nasal intubation and hypopharyngeal approaches; (5) the relationship to the larynx — the fossa lies lateral to the laryngeal inlet and belongs to the hypopharyngeal (laryngopharyngeal) region, not to the laryngeal framework. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in otolaryngology, head and neck surgery, and radiology. e.g.: piriform fossa foreign body impaction described in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; piriform fossa evaluation during a videofluoroscopic swallow study; the piriform fossa as a subsite of hypopharyngeal carcinoma in the AJCC TNM staging, 8th edition | not: the laryngeal inlet (the midline opening between the vocal folds and aryepiglottic folds, not a fossa); the postcricoid region (the midline hypopharyngeal region below the vocal folds, medial to the fossae); the esophagus (the muscular tube below the laryngopharynx) [formal: sinus piriformis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: thyroarytenoid-muscle
payload.scope: People made the thyroarytenoid muscle construct to map the paired intrinsic laryngeal muscles that modulate vocal fold tension and length, so that clinicians can diagnose and treat voice disorders involving muscle imbalance.

definition.body: The thyroarytenoid muscle is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the paired intrinsic laryngeal muscles spanning from the inner thyroid cartilage to the arytenoid cartilages, modulating vocal fold tension and length during phonation. Parameters: (1) the origin — anterior inner surface of the thyroid cartilage angle; (2) the insertion — lateral surface and muscular process of the arytenoid cartilage; (3) the fiber orientation — oblique fibers converging from anterior to posterior; (4) the subdivisions — thyroidarytenoid (muscular) portion and vocalis (medial) portion; (5) the innervation — recurrent laryngeal nerve supplying both portions. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in otolaryngology and speech science. e.g.: the thyroarytenoid muscle as described in Gray's Anatomy, 51st edition; thyroarytenoid hypertrophy on fiberoptic laryngoscopy; thyroarytenoid muscle biopsy for laryngeal dystonia assessment | not: the vocalis muscle (the medial vocal fold portion of the thyroarytenoid, distinct in its fiber orientation); the cricothyroid muscle (the tensor muscle spanning cricoid to thyroid, opposite action) [formal: musculus thyroarytenoideus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The posterior cricoarytenoid muscle is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the paired intrinsic laryngeal muscles originating from the posterior cricoid lamina and inserting into the muscular process of the arytenoid cartilage, serving as the sole abductors of the vocal folds during inspiration. definition.body: The cricothyroid muscle is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the paired extrinsic laryngeal muscles connecting the cricoid cartilage to the thyroid cartilage, serving as the primary tensor of the vocal folds during phonation. Parameters: (1) the origin — anterior and inferior surface of the cricoid cartilage arch; (2) the insertion — inferior horn and lower border of the thyroid cartilage lamina; (3) the fiber orientation — oblique fibers ascending and laterally directed; (4) the action — tilts the thyroid cartilage forward relative to the cricoid, elongating and tensing the vocal folds; (5) the innervation — external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. payload.name: arytenoid-cartilage
payload.scope: People made the arytenoid cartilage construct to map and categorize the paired pyramidal cartilages atop the cricoid lamina whose rotation and muscle attachments control vocal fold adduction and abduction, so that surgeons can identify these landmarks for laryngeal surgery and voice disorder treatment.

definition.body: The arytenoid cartilage is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps each of the paired pyramidal cartilages sitting atop the cricoid cartilage's posterior lamina, whose position and rotation control the adduction and abduction of the vocal folds through their muscular processes. Parameters: (1) the pyramidal shape — three surfaces (laryngeal, muscular, and base), an apex pointing posteriorly, and a base articulating with the cricoid; (2) the laryngeal surface — concave, facing the laryngeal lumen, receiving the lateral cricoarytenoid muscle anteriorly; (3) the muscular process — a lateral projection from the base, serving as the insertion point for the posterior and lateral cricoarytenoid muscles; (4) the articular facet — on the inferior surface for the synovial cricoarytenoid joint with the cricoid lamina; (5) the apex — a narrow posterior projection giving attachment to the aryepiglottic fold. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, laryngology classification systems, and surgical atlases. e.g.: the arytenoid cartilages described in Gray's Anatomy, 51st edition; arytenoidectomy surgical procedure for bilateral vocal fold paralysis; arytenoid cartilage fracture on CT imaging after intubation trauma | not: the cricoid cartilage (the complete ring-shaped cartilage forming the inferior framework of the larynx); cartilage of Wrisberg (a small nodular cartilage at the posterior commissure) [formal: cartilago arytaenoidea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: superior-laryngeal-nerve
payload.scope: People made the superior laryngeal nerve construct to map and categorize the branch of the vagus nerve that divides into internal and external branches to provide sensory innervation above the vocal folds and motor innervation to the cricothyroid muscle, so that clinicians can diagnose laryngeal sensory deficits and cricothyroid dysfunction.

definition.body: The superior laryngeal nerve is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the second major branch of the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X), which descends in the neck to divide into the internal branch (sensory to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds) and the external branch (motor to the cricothyroid muscle). Parameters: (1) the origin — arises from the inferior ganglion of the vagus nerve at the level of the inferior salivary nucleus; (2) the course — descends on the side of the pharynx between the internal carotid artery and the pharyngeal wall; (3) the internal branch — pierces the thyrohyoid membrane to provide sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds and the piriform fossa; (4) the external branch — descends on the larynx surface, supplying the cricothyroid muscle and the superior laryngeal ganglion. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, laryngology atlases, and surgical protocols for thyroid and neck surgery. e.g.: the superior laryngeal nerve anatomy described in Gray's Anatomy, 51st edition; internal branch injury assessed by laryngeal sensory testing with air-puff; external branch injury diagnosed by laryngeal electromyography showing cricothyroid denervation | not: the recurrent-laryngeal-nerve; the vagus-nerve [formal: nervus laryngeus superior | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: pre-epiglottic-space
payload.scope: People made the pre-epiglottic space construct to map the fat-filled region anterior to the epiglottis that provides a pathway for tumor spread in laryngeal carcinoma, so that radiologists and head and neck surgeons can assess the extent of supraglottic cancers for staging and surgical planning.

definition.body: The pre-epiglottic space is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the fat-filled potential space anterior to the epiglottis, bounded by the thyroepiglottic ligament posteriorly, that permits tumor spread assessment in laryngeal carcinoma staging. Parameters: (1) the boundaries — anteriorly by the thyrohyoid membrane and hyoepiglottic ligament, posteriorly by the thyroepiglottic ligament, superiorly by the entrance to the larynx at the level of the epiglottic tip, and laterally by the paraglottic space; (2) the contents — predominantly adipose tissue with loose connective tissue, lymphatic channels, and perivascular fat spaces that permit tumor extension; (3) the shape — roughly triangular in cross-section, wider at its superior aspect tapering inferiorly; (4) the imaging appearance — fat density on CT and intermediate signal on T1-weighted MRI, with loss of normal fat planes indicating tumor invasion. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in head and neck radiology, laryngeal cancer staging systems, and surgical planning for supraglottic laryngectomy. e.g.: the pre-epiglottic space evaluated on axial CT in the AJCC staging of supraglottic carcinoma; the pre-epiglottic fat plane disrupted on MRI in a patient with T3 supraglottic cancer; the pre-epiglottic space dissection during an open supraglottic laryngectomy | not: the paraglottic space (the deeper fat-filled space lateral to the laryngeal ventricle, not anterior to the epiglottis); the thyroepiglottic ligament (the fibrous band forming the posterior boundary of the space, not the space itself) [formal: spatium praeepiglotticum | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.scope: People made the vocal ligament construct to map and categorize the elastic fiber band forming the core of the vocal fold, so that clinicians can identify this structure in vocal surgery and understand its role in phonation.

definition.body: The vocal ligament is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the free upper border of the conus elasticus, forming the rigid core of the vocal fold that vibrates during phonation. Parameters: (1) the composition — dense irregular connective tissue with abundant elastic fibers arranged in a sheet that thickens to form the ligament; (2) the attachments — anteriorly at the angle of the thyroid cartilage just below the laryngeal prominence, posteriorly at the vocal process of the arytenoid cartilage; (3) the layered relationship — the deepest layer of the vocal fold's lamina propria (intermediate layer), superficial to the vocalis muscle and deep to the superficial lamina propria (Reinke's space); (4) the free edge — the medial margin forming the vibrating body of the vocal fold, defining the glottal chink during phonation; (5) the functional stiffness — the ligament provides the tensile framework that determines the fundamental frequency of vibration when tensioned by the cricothyroid and intrinsic laryngeal muscles. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, laryngology classification systems, and surgical atlases. e.g.: the vocal ligament described in Gray's Anatomy, 51st edition; the vocal ligament visible during microlaryngeal surgery as the bright white band within the vocal fold; the vocal ligament tension altered during thyroplasty type III surgery for vocal fold paralysis | not: the vocal fold (the complete mucosal structure including epithelium, lamina propria layers, and muscle); the vestibular fold (the false vocal cord situated superior to the vocal fold) [formal: ligamentum vocale | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]
